The complexity of IMRT planning requires sophisticated algorithms to solve the different optimisation problems that arise in the context of IMRT treatment planning. One of those optimisation problems is the Direct Aperture Optimisation (DAO). The DAO problem aims to find a set of ap- erture shapes for each beam angle to enhance precision and improve clinical outcomes. However, this process is computationally intensive and thus, heuristic approaches have been proposed to balance computational efficiency and solution quality, offering nearly optimal solutions within clinically acceptable times. This systematic literature review aims to trace the development and application of heuristic algorithms for the DAO problem in the context of IMRT over the past two decades. We synthesised 41 studies published be- tween 2002 and 2023, sourced from seven major databases (ACM, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, ScienceDirect, Springer, Scopus, and Web of Science). The review highlights key trends, innovations, and future directions in using heuristic methods for DAO, providing valuable insights for researchers and practitioners in radiotherapy optimisation. Keywords Direct aperture optimisation · Intensity-modulated radiation therapy · Literature review 1 Introduction Intensity-modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT) is a radiotherapy technique widely applied in cancer treatment. In IMRT, the region of the patient’s body where cancerous cells are located (planning target volume or PTV) is irradiated from a set of beam angles using a linear accelerator (linac, see Fig. 1; Cho 2018). IMRT has emerged as a prominent treatment modality (Daly 2020), a 2023 report from Emergen Research highlights the growth of the global IMRT market, valued at $2.21 billion in 2022. It is projected to continue expanding, Extended author information available on the last page of the article 1 3 3 Page 2 of 20 M. Moyano et al. F ig. 1 Linear accelerator (Tello- Valenzuela et al. 2023) with a compound annual growth rate of 5.4%, driven by increasing government incentives and preference for non-invasive cancer treatments (Research 2023). A distinctive feature of IMRT is that the radiation delivered to the patient can be modulated using a physical device called a multi-leaf collimator (MLC). Such modulation is significant for tumours with non- convex shapes in difficult anatomical situations. The IMRT technique enables the delivery of an optimal radiation dose to the tumour while minimising exposure to surrounding healthy organs (Hong et al. 2005). However, finding a treatment plan that balances the desired dose to the tumour and minimal side effects on surrounding organs is highly complex. The planning process for the IMRT is complex, and to generate a treatment plan, this process is usually divided into three sequential sub-problems, namely: beam angle optimisa- tion (BAO), fluence map optimisation (FMO), and multi-leaf collimator sequencing (MLC) (Cao et al. 2009). The BAO problem aims to determine the best beam angle configuration (BAC). Once a BAC is chosen, the FMO calculates the intensities to find the optimal treat- ment plan for the BAC. Finally, the set of deliverable aperture shapes and intensities of the MLC must be calculated (MLC sequencing problem) for the treatment plan. This sequential approach ends up with a treatment plan consisting of a large set of aper- ture shapes (with their corresponding intensity values) (Salari et al. 2011). Unfortunately, having too many apertures and larger intensity values per aperture means longer treatment times. Longer treatment times are undesirable as they require patients to remain on the couch for extended periods, increasing the risk of inaccuracies in treatment delivery due to patient movement (Dzierma et al. 2014) and reducing the number of patients that can be treated daily. Additionally, the total delivery time of a treatment plan, which comprises the beam-on time (BoT, the total time a patient is exposed to radiation) and the time needed by both the linac and the MLC to move between beam angles and achieve the next aperture shape (decomposition time), further contributes to the overall treatment duration (Ahuja and Hamacher 2005; Baatar et al. 2005). To get treatments with fewer times, the number of apertures and the beam-on time must be reduced. To this end, treatment planners usually simplify the treatment plan by round- ing the intensities at each beam angle to some predefined values. This simplification of the optimal plan allows the delivery of a treatment plan using fewer deliverable aperture shapes and shorter BoT. However, this simplification also reduces the quality of the treatment plan (Rocha et al. 2012). Thus, it seems reasonable to incorporate some MLC sequencing consid- 1 3 Heuristics for the direct aperture optimisation in intensity modulated… Page 3 of 20 3 erations into the FMO problem so that the optimal intensities found during its optimisation process can be directly delivered to the patient without any further adjustment. To address this issue, the direct aperture optimisation (DAO) problem was proposed by Shepard et al. (2002). The DAO problem aims to simultaneously optimise the intensities and aperture shapes for each beam ray in the BAC. Hence, their goal is to address and solve the FMO problem, considering the constraint on the number of deliverable apertures and the physical constraints related to the MLC sequencing. Therefore, after solving the DAO problem, we no longer need the leaves sequencing procedure. The DAO problem involves two steps: aperture shape optimisation and aperture weight optimisation (Romeijn et al. 2005). The first step includes calculating the deliverable aperture that provides the most considerable potential improvement in the objective function, and then this one is added to the treatment plan. In the second step, gradient-based optimisation methods are typically used to optimise the aperture weights. Compared to the sequential approach, the quality of the treatment plan obtained by the DAO is considerably improved (Ludlum and Xia 2009). Over the past two decades, significant research has been conducted to develop and refine heuristic methods for DAO in IMRT. This article aims to present a clear picture of the state of the art of the methods used for DAO in IMRT. To this end, a systematic literature review (SLR) is presented. This SLR was carried out following the process proposed by Keele et al. (2007). This method guarantees that the review’s outcome is verifiable and repeatable by other researchers. Also, to ensure the quality of the review, we have incorporated the check- list of elements proposed by PRISMA methodology (Page et al. 2021). The findings of this review offer valuable insights for researchers, clinicians, and poli- cymakers interested in leveraging heuristics to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of DAO in IMRT. This review considered 41 studies published from 2000 to 2023. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive review conducted in this field, and we aim our study to serve as a helpful resource for other researchers working in this area, helping to identify potential approaches and future trends. The article is structured into four main sections. Section 2 describes the methodology used in the SLR. Section 3 details the selection of papers in the SLR. Section 4 answers the research questions outlined in the first section. Finally, Sect. 5 concludes with a summary of findings and insights derived from the review. 2 Research methodology As mentioned, this SLR was carried out following the process proposed by Keele et al. We detail the process followed for this document. 2.1 Research questions We formulated three primary research questions to cover every topic of interest in this systematic literature review (see Table 1). These questions consider relevant and general aspects necessary for comprehending the concepts that we think are important for this SLR. The RQ1 focuses on identifying the heuristic methods applied to the DAO problem and their main characteristics, providing a foundation for understanding the algorithmic diversity and methodological innovations in the field. The RQ2 addresses the objective functions used in the optimisation models, which is crucial as the formulation of these functions directly influ- ences the behaviour, convergence, and clinical utility of the proposed heuristics. Further- more, having insights into the mathematical properties of the objective functions considered to solve the DAO problem helps practitioners to better decide which heuristic methods are most appropriate for a given context. The RQ3 explores the types of cancer cases addressed by DAO methods, allowing an assessment of the anatomical and clinical contexts in which these heuristics have been tested. Finally, RQ3.1 examines the datasets used in the literature, highlighting issues of reproducibility, data availability, and benchmarking practices. 2.2 Data sources and search strategies To conduct this systematic literature review, we searched for scientific papers on seven databases: ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore Digital Library, PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, Springer Link and Web of Science. What methods have been used for the DAO problem, and what characteristics do they have? Several heuristics have been used to solve the Direct Aperture Optimisation (DAO) prob- lem, each offering unique advantages. The first algorithm proposed was simulated annealing by Shepard et al. (2002), which selects random variables and modifies them using a Gauss- ian distribution, offering a straightforward yet practical approach to exploring the solu- tion space. Li et al. (2003) introduced a hybrid method using a conjugate gradient method to determine segment numbers for each beam and initialise segment shapes, and then, a genetic algorithm that optimises the aperture shapes, and a conjugate gradient method that optimises the associated intensities. Cotrutz and Xing (2003) also utilised a genetic algo- rithm but focused solely on optimising aperture shapes and intensities. Beaulieu et al. (2004) developed a method to automatically generate anatomy-based apertures, simplifying treat- ment verification and imposing mechanical constraints to ensure dosimetric reliability. Bed- ford and Webb (2006) proposed feedback optimisation, which uses random and constrained perturbations to narrow to enhance efficiency and precision. In their later work, Bedford and Webb (2007) proposed a heuristic that directly optimised the spatial distribution and 1 3 3 Page 10 of 20 M. Moyano et al. shapes of beam apertures, improving planning efficiency by bypassing intermediate steps. Bogner et al. (2009) introduced the Direct Monte Carlo Optimisation, where they integrate inverse kernel dose calculation with simulated annealing, allowing direct optimisation with- out intermediary fluence map steps, thus preserving plan quality. Cao et al. (2014) combined genetic algorithms and conjugate gradient methods, encoding the aperture shape as a 0/1 matrix and adjusting it using the genetic algorithm, then optimising the aperture weights with the conjugate gradient method. Pakela et al. (2020) introduced the Quantum Tunnel Annealing algorithm, which incorporates quantum fluctuations to avoid local minima and achieves faster convergence. Stochastic local search algorithms have also been applied; for instance, Pérez Cáceres et al. (2019, 2021) proposed iterative local search algorithms with dual search mechanisms, while Moyano and Cabrera-Guerrero (2020) offered hybrid local search strategies com- bined with mathematical programming to reduce the number of apertures and beam-on times. Ripsman et al. (2022) developed a robust DAO model that considers the uncertainty in breathing motion. They employed a candidate plan generation algorithm to manage the complexity of the problem, ensuring robust and reliable treatment plans despite patient movement. Fallahi et al. (2022) formulated a mixed-integer nonlinear mathematical model and used particle swarm optimisation (PSO) and differential evolution (DE) to solve it, leveraging metaheuristic strengths for effective DAO problem-solving. Tello-Valenzuela et al. (2023) proposed a hybrid approach integrating PSO with mathematical programming. Their method optimises the intensities and shapes of apertures through PSO, while a math- ematical programming technique fine-tunes the aperture intensities. A reparation heuristic is introduced to improve the aperture shapes that minimally impact the treatment plan. This heuristic adjusts aperture shapes to improve their contribution to the treatment plan, ensur- ing that apertures with near-zero intensities are replaced with more effective ones. Tian et al. (2023) proposed a method leveraging evolutionary computation with customised variation operators. The method employs customised crossover and mutation operators designed to accelerate convergence and ensure the validity of treatment plans, thereby eliminating the need for cumbersome repair operations. Additionally, the approach incorporates an objec- tive reduction strategy to group and reduce the number of objectives automatically. Besides the incomplete techniques presented, exact methods have also been proposed to solve the DAO problem. Preciado-Walters et al. (2004) proposed a coupled column gen- eration heuristic, which alternates between generating patterns for desirable intensity maps and reducing the computational burden of enforcing dose-volume constraints. Preciado- Walters et al. (2006) refined this approach by combining two-column generation techniques, employing a cubic function for smooth MLC shapes and a feedback optimisation method to ensure viable aperture shapes, thereby enhancing treatment planning efficiency and quality. In the work of Romeijn et al. (2005), the gradients of the objective function are employed to formulate a network flow, which can be solved as a shortest path problem. Solving this sub-problem generates an optimal aperture shape meeting machine-specific requirements. Then, the master problem computed the intensity of each determined aperture. Men et al. (2007) expanded this approach by incorporating more general treatment plan evaluation criteria and extending the method to MLC systems capable of delivering only rectangular apertures. Men et al. (2010) further enhanced this algorithm with a GPU-based implementa- tion, significantly reducing the computational time for generating treatment plans. Carlsson (2008) proposed a technique that generates a sequence of treatment plans with increasing 1 3 Heuristics for the direct aperture optimisation in intensity modulated… Page 11 of 20 3 segments, combining segment generation with direct step-and-shoot (DSS) optimisation. This method begins with generating initial segments from the target projection onto the isocenter plane for each beam. These segments are iteratively refined through DSS optimi- sation, where leaf positions and segment weights are optimised simultaneously. A column generation method is used to guide new segment creation based on the gradient of the objec- tive function. This method continuously adjusts segment shapes and weights, improving plan quality. Salari et al. (2011) integrated dose calculation inaccuracies from the tongue- and-groove effect into the optimisation process, creating robust treatment plans resilient to these uncertainties. Cassioli and Unkelbach (2013) formulated the dose aperture model as a piecewise-linear function concerning aperture leaf positions, allowing efficient gradient computation for local leaf position refinement. This approach enhances the precision of aperture adjustments. Jie et al. (2015) proposed a multi-phase DAO method for inverse planning in radiotherapy, aiming to improve efficiency and plan quality. The technique initialises each beam direction with a single aperture and optimises the aperture weights using the Fletcher-Reeves conjugate gradient method. New apertures are then generated by solving the shortest path problem to further decrease the objective function value. This method optimises flu- ence maps, and MLC segment shapes iteratively, with indices assigned to each voxel and beamlet for efficient optimisation. This interactive planning process leads to improved plan quality and reduced treatment time. Nguyen et al. This method uses a proximal-class, first-order primal- dual solver to alternate between updating fluence maps and delivery segments, ensuring high-quality optimisation. MacFarlane et al. (2019) presented a fast inverse dose optimisa- tion algorithm using direct matrix inversion and a second-order Taylor series expansion to reformulate the objective function. This method quickly finds the global minimum, improv- ing optimisation speed and accuracy. Some authors have addressed the multi-objective DAO problem by extending some of the methods proposed for its single-objective version. Salari and Romeijn (2012) incorporated beam-on time as a measure of delivery efficiency into treatment plan optimisation, formulat- ing a bi-criteria convex DAO model to balance plan quality and beam-on time. This bi-cri- teria approach allows for the characterisation of Pareto-efficient treatment plans, optimising the trade-offs between different evaluation criteria. Salari and Unkelbach (2013) proposed a multi-objective column generation approach for DAO. The method employs a multi-criteria convex model to optimise objectives simultaneously using a column generation algorithm that iteratively adds promising apertures to improve the current solution set. Integrating Pareto surface navigation allows the exploration of trade-offs between objectives, helping to identify a diverse set of Pareto-optimal treatment plans. One advantage of this approach is that it also ensures using the same set of apertures across different plans, avoiding leaf sequencing. Fredriksson and Bokrantz (2013) proposed a technique for deliverable Pareto surface navigation, combining shared and individual apertures. This method involves direct step-and-shoot optimisation of multiple plans simultaneously, with constraints ensuring that some apertures are identical across all plans while others remain individual. The apertures are optimised through a gradient-based approach, adjusting leaf positions and segment weights to meet dose distribution objectives while adhering to MLC hardware limitations. Long et al. (2012) proposed a technique based on lexicographic ordering called sensitiv- ity analysis in lexicographic ordering (SALO). This method involves generating a pool of clinically relevant apertures, determining patient-specific treatment planning goals through bi-criteria optimisation problems, and then creating a final treatment plan that meets these goals while minimising a single objective function. This structured and prioritised optimisa- tion process ensures clinical relevance and effectiveness. (2022), which define different types of methods used in DAO: Stochastic search methods, Gradient-based leaf methods, Columns generation methods and Segmenta- tion of Fluence map. In the literature, several criteria have been used to guide the optimisation process in IMRT. As seen in the survey by Ehrgott et al. (2008), there exist different forms of objective func- tions that have been used in IMRT: voxel-based penalties, voxel-based deposited dose, and equivalent uniform dose, among others. These mathematical models are divided into five categories: feasibility problems, linear models, nonlinear models, mixed integer models and multi-objective models. However, since the DAO problem has a different representation than the FMO problem, apertures are generally considered as binary variables (see Shepard et al. (2002)). Thus, the vast majority of the models implemented for the DAO problem belong to the mixed integer programming models category defined by Ehrgott et al. (2008). Given this context, we decided to categorise the studies based on the type of objective function used rather than their mathematical features. Additionally, considering that some methods focus on feasibility instead of using an objective function, we included this aspect in our categorisation. We have grouped them into feasibility, mixed integer linear problems (MILP), and mixed integer non-linear problems (MINLP), as shown in Table 7. Table 7 shows that most of the revised studies (95.1%) used a dosimetric function (Voxel-based deposited dose and Voxel-based penalise). Also, most works we analysed use nonlinear functions to evaluate their algorithms (82.9%). What types of cancer has DAO been used on? As mentioned in several works, IMRT has been used to treat different types of cancer, such as prostate, head-and-neck, lung, brain, gastrointestinal, and breast, among others. How- ever, the heuristics proposed in the DAO literature have been applied to limited types of cancer cases. This review identifies 15 types of cancer where heuristics have been applied, as shown in Table 8. Additionally, there exist several authors who use phantom cases to test their heuristics (Shepard et al. 2002; Li et al. 2003; Cotrutz and Xing 2003; Bedford and Webb 2006, 2007; Bogner et al. 2009; Zeng et al. 2018; MacFarlane et al. 2019). However, less than 22% of the studies use one of these public datasets and have, in general, only four types of cancer, namely prostate, head-and-neck, liver and lung. In general, we can say that datasets in Table 9 are valuable for validating the effectiveness and efficiency of new algorithms in a standardised and reproducible manner, enhancing the credibility and comparability of research outcomes. 5 Conclusions This systematic literature review has provided a comprehensive overview of the various methods used to address the DAO problem in IMRT. The review meticulously followed the methodology proposed by Keele et al. (2007) and included elements of the PRISMA methodology proposed by Page et al. (2021), ensuring that the findings were verifiable and repeatable by other researchers. From the analysis performed in this review, diverse methods employed in DAO were identified, each with unique advantages. The reviewed techniques ranged from traditional stochastic methods (like simulated annealing and genetic algorithms) and exact methods (like column generation) to modern approaches such as quantum tunnel annealing, neural network-based optimisation, and hybrid methods. It is interesting to note that, despite the variety of methods used to solve the DAO problem in the literature, most of the methods presented in this study are based on column generation methods (48.7%) and stochastic search (41.4%). Notably, although IMRT is inherently a multi-objective problem (Ham- acher and Küfer 2002), only a few studies on this review have explored this perspective in depth (9.74%). Also, it is interesting to note that the vast majority of the studies (95.1%) considered in our review use dosimetric objective functions. In contrast, only three studies used the gen- eralised equivalent uniform dose (gEUD), and no study considered biological optimisation 1 3 Heuristics for the direct aperture optimisation in intensity modulated… Page 17 of 20 3 criteria like tumour control probability or normal tissue complication probability. Moreover, integrating multiple types of objective functions within the same model (as Mueller et al. 2022 does it) represents a significant future research direction that needs to be considered. Another relevant information is the types of cancer cases used to test these methods. Regarding this, we have that prostate cases (65.8%) are the cancer type most used in the revised studies, followed by head-and-neck (41.4%), lung (12.1%) and liver (9.7%) cases. A notable number of studies also utilised phantom cases for testing (8 out of 41, i.e. 19.5% ). In addition, it was observed that most datasets used in these studies are private, which makes it impossible to reproduce and compare their results to other proposed methods in the literature. Only a few studies used publicly available datasets like TROTS, CORT, and CERR. Unfortunately, these datasets only consider a few types of cancer cases. JSON: Name: hybrid_column_generation_neuraldao_multiobjective Title: Hybrid column-generation with a neural-dose surrogate for multi-objective direct aperture optimisation in intensity-modulated radiation therapy Short Hypothesis: Integrating a neural-network-based dose surrogate into a multi-objective column-generation DAO framework causes statistically significant improvements in dose conformity and reductions in beam-on time compared to standard column-generation DAO using analytic dose models and single-objective optimisation. Related Work: Existing DAO approaches cluster into column-generation methods, stochastic search/metaheuristics, gradient-based leaf optimisation, fluence segmentation-based approaches, and lexicographic/priority ordering schemes. Column-generation methods provide systematic aperture pool expansion and strong solution quality but rely on expensive dose calculations in the pricing step and are typically used with single-objective formulations. Stochastic and hybrid metaheuristics offer flexibility in aperture shape search but often require extensive tuning and have variable reproducibility. Gradient-based leaf methods and segmentation integrate continuous adjustments but can be trapped in local minima and struggle with machine constraints. Recent works have started using learned dose surrogates and hybrid algorithms separately, and a few studies consider multi-objective trade-offs, but limitations remain: many methods use simplified dose models that create delivered/planned dose discrepancies, few algorithms jointly optimise multiple clinical objectives within the column-generation paradigm, datasets are frequently private and cancer-case diversity is narrow (prostate-dominated), and computational cost or scalability is rarely addressed comprehensively. Abstract: Direct aperture optimisation (DAO) for IMRT seeks deliverable aperture shapes and weights that balance competing clinical objectives under machine constraints, but current column-generation and heuristic methods are limited by costly dose evaluations, single-objective formulations, and mismatches between optimised and delivered dose. We propose a hybrid DAO pipeline that embeds a neural-network dose surrogate into the column-generation pricing problem and performs explicit multi-objective optimisation to produce a Pareto set of deliverable plans. The core contributions are: (1) a surrogate-accelerated pricing operator that replaces repeated high-fidelity dose calls during aperture generation, (2) an integrated multi-objective column-generation mechanism that exposes plan trade-offs while reusing a common aperture set, and (3) an evaluation protocol that validates plan quality by recomputing high-fidelity delivered doses and reporting Pareto-front metrics and delivery-efficiency measures. Expected outcomes include faster aperture generation, improved Pareto-front coverage with lower beam-on times, and closer agreement between optimised and delivered doses compared to baseline DAO algorithms. Experiments: Datasets: TROTS benchmark set (120 cases: prostate/head-and-neck/liver), CORT dataset (≈10 cases, prostate/head-and-neck/liver), CERR subset (10 cases, prostate/head-and-neck), Shanxi hospital set (9 cases, prostate/head-and-neck). Split: for surrogate training use pooled 70% of cases (stratified by site) and evaluate on 30% holdout; perform cross-dataset generalisation tests (train on TROTS+CORT, test on CERR+Shanxi). Baselines: (A) standard column-generation DAO using analytic/deterministic dose influence matrices, single-objective; (B) column-generation DAO with high-fidelity dose in pricing (no surrogate); (C) stochastic DAO (simulated annealing/genetic) representative; (D) NeuralDAO (learned-dose integrated but single-objective). Proposed method: multi-objective column-generation with neural-dose surrogate. Evaluation metrics: conformity index (CI), homogeneity index (HI), mean and max doses to specified OARs, gEUD for selected structures, beam-on time (BoT), number of apertures, Pareto hypervolume and spread, DVH error between optimised and recomputed high-fidelity dose (L2 and max), computational time for planning (total and per pricing call). Experimental procedure: train neural surrogate to predict voxel doses given aperture set and weights using high-fidelity labels; integrate surrogate into pricing and run column-generation to yield Pareto sets under aperture budget constraints (e.g., 5, 10, 20 apertures). Perform ablations: (1) surrogate vs no-surrogate (high-fidelity pricing), (2) multi-objective vs single-objective optimisation, (3) surrogate accuracy levels (trained on 25%, 50%, 100% of training labels), (4) aperture budget sensitivity (5/10/20). Statistical analysis: paired tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank) on CI, BoT, DVH error across patient cases with significance alpha=0.05; report median and interquartile ranges. Repeatability: run each stochastic baseline 10 seeds; report mean and variance. Risk Factors and Limitations: Neural surrogate bias or insufficient generalisation leading to suboptimal or clinically unsafe aperture proposals; reliance on quality and representativeness of high-fidelity dose labels for surrogate training; reduced interpretability of surrogate-driven pricing decisions compared to analytic dose; potential overfitting to prostate-dominated training sets and degraded performance on less-represented anatomies; surrogate integration may change optimisation landscape and produce Pareto fronts that are artifacts of surrogate error; extra computational cost and engineering to train and validate surrogates, possibly negating runtime gains for small case counts; limitations in modelling patient motion and interfractional variability (not explicitly addressed); deliverability constraints of different linac/MLC hardware may limit generalisability; regulatory and clinical-acceptance hurdles due to learned components in treatment planning; dependence on availability of public high-fidelity datasets for reproducible benchmarking.
